title: Genesis 1 — When the Elohim began to shape

paragraphs.text: בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים אֵ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם וְאֵ֥ת הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: When the Elohim began to shape the skies and the land—

paragraphs.commentary:
**Three load-bearing choices in one verse.**

*Bereshit* is grammatically a construct form **without** the definite article — בְּרֵאשִׁית means "in beginning-of", not "in **the** beginning" (which would require בָּרֵאשִׁית). The verse is a temporal clause introducing v2 and v3, not a freestanding declaration. The Rashi-favoured reading, also adopted by NJPS, NRSV, and most modern scholarly translations, treats the construct as it stands: *When the Elohim began to shape …* The traditional "In the beginning" carries a *creatio-ex-nihilo* doctrinal commitment the Hebrew doesn't grammatically support. Restoring the construct lets the text describe a project beginning, not the absolute origin of all matter.

*Bara* is one of three creation verbs Genesis 1 deploys deliberately (with *asah* "make" and *yatsar* "form"). Standard translations flatten all three into "create/make", losing the pattern. *Bara* in the Qal denotes shaping or fashioning; the Piel of the same root means "cut out, fashion". Rendering as **shape** preserves the verb's distinctness without inserting a metaphysical claim either way. The verb returns in v21 (sea-creatures) and v27 (humankind) — three categorical moments out of dozens of creative acts in the chapter.

*Elohim* is grammatically masculine plural (-im ending). The singular "God" is a theological smoothing inherited from the LXX's choice to render with singular Θεός. The plural form is preserved untranslated. Plural verbs and pronouns governing the Elohim are flagged where they appear (see v26).

*Shamayim* is grammatically dual (the -ayim ending). Hebrew has no singular form for sky/heaven. **Skies** preserves the dual. *Eretz* covers a spectrum from "patch of ground" to "inhabited territory". The capital-E "Earth" (the planet) is a 17th-century English meaning the Hebrew doesn't carry. **Land** is closer to the register.

paragraphs.text: וְהָאָ֗רֶץ הָיְתָ֥ה תֹ֙הוּ֙ וָבֹ֔הוּ וְחֹ֖שֶׁךְ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י תְה֑וֹם וְר֣וּחַ אֱלֹהִ֔ים מְרַחֶ֖פֶת עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הַמָּֽיִם׃

i18n.en: —the land being wasteland and emptiness, with darkness over the face of the deep, and the breath of the Elohim hovering over the face of the waters—

paragraphs.commentary:
**The single most contested choice in this chapter.**

*Ruach Elohim* — רוּחַ has three lexical fields: **breath**, **wind**, **spirit**. Hebrew does not disambiguate; context is the only guide. KJV/ASV's "Spirit of God" is a Trinitarian-tradition reading retrojected onto Gen 1:2; the Hebrew supports "wind" (NJPS: "a wind from God"), "breath", or "spirit" equally. The verb that follows — *merachefet* — specifically denotes **hovering/fluttering** (cf. Deut 32:11, an eagle hovering over its young). Wind hovers; breath hovers; *Spirit* doesn't, in any natural register. The WoH choice is **breath of the Elohim hovering**, preserving the verb's bird-image and the verse's physical/atmospheric register without importing a Trinitarian doctrinal claim.

*Tohu vavohu* — KJV "without form and void" reads philosophical (Aristotelian matter without form); the Hebrew is concrete. The pair appears together in Jer 4:23 describing a post-disaster depopulated landscape, and in Isa 34:11 (similar). **Wasteland and emptiness** preserves the alliterative pair (the -ohu / -ohu echo) and the concrete imagery.

*Tehom* is etymologically and conceptually cognate with Akkadian *tiāmtu* — the same root behind **Tiamat** of the *Enuma Elish*, where the goddess is the primordial salt-sea. Genesis has demythologized the term but preserved the word. The link is recorded in the glossary; the translation itself stays measured ("the deep").

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֖ים יְהִ֣י א֑וֹר וַֽיְהִי־אֽוֹר׃

i18n.en: The Elohim said, "Let there be light"; and there was light.

paragraphs.commentary: Under the construct reading begun in v1, v3 is the **main clause** of the v1–v3 temporal structure: *When the Elohim began to shape ... the land being wasteland and emptiness ... the Elohim said, "Let there be light"*. The verse-initial "And" of older English translations is dropped — this is the first clause, not a continuation.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֧רְא אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶת־הָא֖וֹר כִּי־ט֑וֹב וַיַּבְדֵּ֣ל אֱלֹהִ֔ים בֵּ֥ין הָא֖וֹר וּבֵ֥ין הַחֹֽשֶׁךְ׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim saw that the light was good; and the Elohim separated between the light and the darkness.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֨א אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ לָאוֹר֙ י֔וֹם וְלַחֹ֖שֶׁךְ קָ֣רָא לָ֑יְלָה וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם אֶחָֽד׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And the Elohim called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, day one.

paragraphs.commentary: *Yom echad* — **day one**, cardinal *echad*, not the ordinal *rishon*. Hebrew uses the cardinal uniquely for day one, then switches to ordinals (*sheni, shlishi, …*) for days 2–6. Most English translations smooth to "first day" / "a second day" which loses the deliberate signaling. The numbered-day pattern in Hebrew is bookended: cardinal *echad* opens, definite *ha-shishi* ("the sixth day") closes (v31).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֔ים יְהִ֥י רָקִ֖יעַ בְּת֣וֹךְ הַמָּ֑יִם וִיהִ֣י מַבְדִּ֔יל בֵּ֥ין מַ֖יִם לָמָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said, "Let there be a dome in the midst of the waters, and let it separate between waters and waters."

paragraphs.commentary: *Raqia* derives from the verb רקע — **to hammer out** (a metal sheet). The ANE cosmology is a solid vault hammered out across the sky to hold back the upper waters (cf. v6–7, where the *raqia* is explicitly placed *between* waters and waters). The LXX renders στερέωμα ("solid/firm thing"), whence Vulgate *firmamentum*, whence English **firmament**. Modern translations soften further to "expanse" (ESV, NIV), which papers over the solid-dome cosmology. The WoH choice is **dome** — accurate to the Hebrew picture, honest about the cosmology, and lets the reader make their own peace with the picture.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֣עַשׂ אֱלֹהִים֮ אֶת־הָרָקִיעַ֒ וַיַּבְדֵּ֗ל בֵּ֤ין הַמַּ֙יִם֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ מִתַּ֣חַת לָרָקִ֔יעַ וּבֵ֣ין הַמַּ֔יִם אֲשֶׁ֖ר מֵעַ֣ל לָרָקִ֑יעַ וַֽיְהִי־כֵֽן׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim made the dome, and separated between the waters which were under the dome and the waters which were above the dome. And it was so.

paragraphs.commentary: **Verb pattern point.** The dome is *made* (*asah*), not *shaped* (*bara*). The chapter alternates the verbs deliberately: *bara* is reserved for v1 (skies and land), v21 (the unprecedented sea-creatures), and v27 (humankind). Everything else — including the dome here — is *asah*. Most English translations interchange the two verbs freely; preserving them apart surfaces the deliberate categorical work the chapter is doing.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֧א אֱלֹהִ֛ים לָֽרָקִ֖יעַ שָׁמָ֑יִם וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם שֵׁנִֽי׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And the Elohim called the dome Skies. And there was evening and there was morning, day two.

paragraphs.commentary: **Note the absence of "the Elohim saw that it was good" on day 2.** This is a textual feature, not an omission, and has drawn rabbinic and modern scholarly comment for centuries. The standard explanations: (1) the project of separating the waters is not complete until day 3, when the dry land appears, so the "good" lands then (v10 closes day 2 *and* day 3's first work with a single "good"); (2) day 2's work is structural plumbing, not a final result. The omission is deliberate and intelligible. The translation preserves the absence without comment in the verse; the lens surfaces it here.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֗ים יִקָּו֨וּ הַמַּ֜יִם מִתַּ֤חַת הַשָּׁמַ֙יִם֙ אֶל־מָק֣וֹם אֶחָ֔ד וְתֵרָאֶ֖ה הַיַּבָּשָׁ֑ה וַֽיְהִי־כֵֽן׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said, "Let the waters under the skies be gathered to one place, and let the dry ground appear." And it was so.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֨א אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ לַיַּבָּשָׁה֙ אֶ֔רֶץ וּלְמִקְוֵ֥ה הַמַּ֖יִם קָרָ֣א יַמִּ֑ים וַיַּ֥רְא אֱלֹהִ֖ים כִּי־טֽוֹב׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim called the dry ground Land, and the gathering of the waters he called Seas. And the Elohim saw that it was good.

paragraphs.commentary: Capitalized **Land** here is a proper name (the Elohim is naming the dry ground), parallel to **Seas**. This is a naming moment within the chapter, distinct from the default-register *eretz* = "land" elsewhere.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֗ים תַּֽדְשֵׁ֤א הָאָ֙רֶץ֙ דֶּ֔שֶׁא עֵ֚שֶׂב מַזְרִ֣יעַ זֶ֔רַע עֵ֣ץ פְּרִ֞י עֹ֤שֶׂה פְּרִי֙ לְמִינ֔וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר זַרְעוֹ־ב֖וֹ עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וַֽיְהִי־כֵֽן׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said, "Let the land sprout vegetation: seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees making fruit according to their kind, in which is their seed, upon the land." And it was so.

paragraphs.text: וַתּוֹצֵ֨א הָאָ֜רֶץ דֶּ֠שֶׁא עֵ֣שֶׂב מַזְרִ֤יעַ זֶ֙רַע֙ לְמִינֵ֔הוּ וְעֵ֧ץ עֹֽשֶׂה־פְּרִ֛י אֲשֶׁ֥ר זַרְעוֹ־ב֖וֹ לְמִינֵ֑הוּ וַיַּ֥רְא אֱלֹהִ֖ים כִּי־טֽוֹב׃

i18n.en: And the land brought forth vegetation: seed-bearing plants according to their kind, and trees making fruit in which is their seed according to their kind. And the Elohim saw that it was good.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם שְׁלִישִֽׁי׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And there was evening and there was morning, day three.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֗ים יְהִ֤י מְאֹרֹת֙ בִּרְקִ֣יעַ הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם לְהַבְדִּ֕יל בֵּ֥ין הַיּ֖וֹם וּבֵ֣ין הַלָּ֑יְלָה וְהָי֤וּ לְאֹתֹת֙ וּלְמ֣וֹעֲדִ֔ים וּלְיָמִ֖ים וְשָׁנִֽים׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said, "Let there be luminaries in the dome of the skies to separate between the day and the night; and let them be for signs and for appointed times, and for days and years;

paragraphs.commentary:
*Meorot* — **luminaries**, not "lights". The Hebrew is a more technical word than *or* (light): it denotes **light-source objects**. The plural form returns through v14–v16 as the cosmos-organizing category that the chapter is positioning here.

*Moadim* — **appointed times**, not "seasons". The Hebrew has a technical calendrical sense — fixed times, festival appointments, predetermined astronomical occasions. The KJV/ASV "seasons" reads natural-cycles (spring/summer/autumn/winter); the Hebrew is structural-calendrical. The luminaries are positioned here as functional time-keepers, not as deities.

paragraphs.text: וְהָי֤וּ לִמְאוֹרֹת֙ בִּרְקִ֣יעַ הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם לְהָאִ֖יר עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וַֽיְהִי־כֵֽן׃

i18n.en: and let them be as luminaries in the dome of the skies, to give light upon the land." And it was so.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֣עַשׂ אֱלֹהִ֔ים אֶת־שְׁנֵ֥י הַמְּאֹרֹ֖ת הַגְּדֹלִ֑ים אֶת־הַמָּא֤וֹר הַגָּדֹל֙ לְמֶמְשֶׁ֣לֶת הַיּ֔וֹם וְאֶת־הַמָּא֤וֹר הַקָּטֹן֙ לְמֶמְשֶׁ֣לֶת הַלַּ֔יְלָה וְאֵ֖ת הַכּוֹכָבִֽים׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim made the two great luminaries: the greater luminary for the governance of the day, and the lesser luminary for the governance of the night; and the stars.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The most polemically charged verse in the chapter.** Hebrew has perfectly good words for **sun** (*shemesh*) and **moon** (*yareach*) and they are not used. Both terms were divinized in surrounding ANE traditions — *Shamash* (the sun god of Babylon, Sippar, Larsa), *Sin* (the Sumero-Akkadian moon god of Ur, Harran). Genesis 1 demythologizes them by naming them only by function: **the greater luminary** to govern day, **the lesser luminary** to govern night. The stars get one terminal half-line, almost as an afterthought ("and the stars"). The deliberate refusal of personal names is the polemic. Preserving "luminary" rather than smoothing back to "sun/moon" is non-optional under the WoH lens.

*Memshelet* — **governance**, a relatively technical political term ("dominion over a territory", "jurisdiction"), not just "rule". The luminaries are granted functional jurisdiction over day and night — the cosmos is being organized into administrative compartments assigned to functional bodies.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּתֵּ֥ן אֹתָ֛ם אֱלֹהִ֖ים בִּרְקִ֣יעַ הַשָּׁמָ֑יִם לְהָאִ֖יר עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim set them in the dome of the skies to give light upon the land,

paragraphs.text: וְלִמְשֹׁל֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם וּבַלַּ֔יְלָה וּֽלֲהַבְדִּ֔יל בֵּ֥ין הָא֖וֹר וּבֵ֣ין הַחֹ֑שֶׁךְ וַיַּ֥רְא אֱלֹהִ֖ים כִּי־טֽוֹב׃

i18n.en: and to rule in the day and in the night, and to separate between the light and the darkness. And the Elohim saw that it was good.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם רְבִיעִֽי׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And there was evening and there was morning, day four.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֔ים יִשְׁרְצ֣וּ הַמַּ֔יִם שֶׁ֖רֶץ נֶ֣פֶשׁ חַיָּ֑ה וְעוֹף֙ יְעוֹפֵ֣ף עַל־הָאָ֔רֶץ עַל־פְּנֵ֖י רְקִ֥יעַ הַשָּׁמָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living beings, and let birds fly above the land across the face of the dome of the skies."

paragraphs.commentary: *Nefesh chayah* — **living being**, not "living creature" or "living soul". *Nefesh* is famously hard: its lexical core is **breath / throat / self / life**, not a Platonic-detachable soul. The KJV "soul" (in Gen 2:7 for *ha-adam*) is the retrojection to avoid; modern Hebrew Bible studies consensus is firmly "being" or "creature". The translation uses **living being** consistently for *nefesh chayah*.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּבְרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֔ים אֶת־הַתַּנִּינִ֖ם הַגְּדֹלִ֑ים וְאֵ֣ת כָּל־נֶ֣פֶשׁ הַֽחַיָּ֣ה ׀ הָֽרֹמֶ֡שֶׂת אֲשֶׁר֩ שָׁרְצ֨וּ הַמַּ֜יִם לְמִֽינֵהֶ֗ם וְאֵ֨ת כָּל־ע֤וֹף כָּנָף֙ לְמִינֵ֔הוּ וַיַּ֥רְא אֱלֹהִ֖ים כִּי־טֽוֹב׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim shaped the great sea-creatures, and every living being that moves, with which the waters swarmed, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And the Elohim saw that it was good.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The verb returns.** The sea-creatures are *shaped* (*bara*), not *made* (*asah*). Why? Because *tanninim* (sea-monsters / great sea-creatures) appears elsewhere in mythological contexts (Job 7:12, Isa 27:1, Ps 74:13) where it denotes rival sea-dragon figures. The deliberate use of *bara* here is a **demythologizing** move — these are *made by the Elohim*, not rivals to it. Preserving *bara* as **shape** lets the reader see the verb pattern across v1 → v21 → v27.

*Taninim* — **great sea-creatures**. KJV "whales" is a domesticating mistranslation that loses the mythological-cousin register entirely; modern translations correctly retain "sea-monsters" or "great sea-creatures". The lens does not need to commit to the mythological reading here; the text has already demythologized.

paragraphs.text: וַיְבָ֧רֶךְ אֹתָ֛ם אֱלֹהִ֖ים לֵאמֹ֑ר פְּר֣וּ וּרְב֗וּ וּמִלְא֤וּ אֶת־הַמַּ֙יִם֙ בַּיַּמִּ֔ים וְהָע֖וֹף יִ֥רֶב בָּאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas; and let the birds multiply on the land."

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם חֲמִישִֽׁי׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And there was evening and there was morning, day five.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֗ים תּוֹצֵ֨א הָאָ֜רֶץ נֶ֤פֶשׁ חַיָּה֙ לְמִינָ֔הּ בְּהֵמָ֥ה וָרֶ֛מֶשׂ וְחַֽיְתוֹ־אֶ֖רֶץ לְמִינָ֑הּ וַֽיְהִי־כֵֽן׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said, "Let the land bring forth living beings according to their kind: cattle, and creeping things, and beasts of the land according to their kind." And it was so.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֣עַשׂ אֱלֹהִים֩ אֶת־חַיַּ֨ת הָאָ֜רֶץ לְמִינָ֗הּ וְאֶת־הַבְּהֵמָה֙ לְמִינָ֔הּ וְאֵ֛ת כָּל־רֶ֥מֶשׂ הָֽאֲדָמָ֖ה לְמִינֵ֑הוּ וַיַּ֥רְא אֱלֹהִ֖ים כִּי־טֽוֹב׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim made the beasts of the land according to their kind, and the cattle according to their kind, and every creeping thing of the ground according to its kind. And the Elohim saw that it was good.

paragraphs.commentary: **Verb pattern note.** Land animals are *made* (*asah*), not *shaped* (*bara*). The chapter has now used *bara* twice (v1, v21) and *asah* many times. The third and final cluster of *bara* arrives in v27 for humankind.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֔ים נַֽעֲשֶׂ֥ה אָדָ֛ם בְּצַלְמֵ֖נוּ כִּדְמוּתֵ֑נוּ וְיִרְדּוּ֩ בִדְגַ֨ת הַיָּ֜ם וּבְע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֗יִם וּבַבְּהֵמָה֙ וּבְכָל־הָאָ֔רֶץ וּבְכָל־הָרֶ֖מֶשׂ הָֽרֹמֵ֥שׂ עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said, "Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the skies, and over the cattle, and over all the land, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the land."

paragraphs.commentary:
**The central textual datum of the chapter, and the most-cited verse of the chapter for the WoH lens.** *Na'aseh* is the cohortative first-person **plural** of *asah* — *let us make*. It is grammatically unambiguous in Hebrew. The pronouns and possessives that follow are also plural: *b'tsalmenu* ("in **our** image"), *ki-dmutenu* ("according to **our** likeness").

Standard theological glosses include:

1. **Plural of majesty** — the royal "we". Ad hoc and not well-attested elsewhere in Hebrew for divine speech; the strongest objection is that *Elohim* never elsewhere governs first-person plural verbs of self-deliberation. Several Jewish commentators (Ibn Ezra, others) have endorsed this read but the textual support is weak.
2. **Trinitarian pre-figuring** — Christian retrojection; not a Hebrew-internal reading.
3. **Divine-council** — the modern scholarly consensus. the Elohim deliberates with attendant divine beings (cf. Job 1:6, Ps 82, 1 Kgs 22:19–22). The council reading reads the plural at face value but diffuses the agency.
4. **Literal plural agency** — the WoH lens reading. the Elohim deliberate as a plural agent in their own right.

The translation does **not** adjudicate. It preserves the grammar. The lens reading is one of the two textually defensible readings (alongside divine-council), and is the one the rest of the WoH corpus operates on.

*Adam* → **humankind**, not "man". *Ha-adam* is a category here, not a personal name (the named individual Adam appears later, in Gen 2–5). Gendered "man" is corrected (NJPS, NRSV both render "humankind"). The naming wordplay with *adamah* ("ground") will surface in Gen 2.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּבְרָ֨א אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ אֶת־הָֽאָדָם֙ בְּצַלְמ֔וֹ בְּצֶ֥לֶם אֱלֹהִ֖ים בָּרָ֣א אֹת֑וֹ זָכָ֥ר וּנְקֵבָ֖ה בָּרָ֥א אֹתָֽם׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim shaped humankind in his image; in the image of the Elohim he shaped him; male and female he shaped them.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The verb pattern peaks: *bara* three times in one verse.** Humankind is *shaped* (*bara*), not just *made* (*asah*). The triple *bara* — once for the act, once for the image-specification, once for the male-and-female dimorphism — bookends the verb pattern of the chapter: v1 (skies and land), v21 (sea-creatures), v27 (humankind ×3). Categorical creation moments only.

**The plural-singular shift v26 → v27.** v26 has plural "Let us make … in **our** image" (*na'aseh … b'tsalmenu*), v27 has singular "in **his** image" (*b'tsalmo*) and singular subject *bara* ×3. The shift is textually real and the lens must address it. The natural reading: deliberative project speech (plural) → executing agency assignment (singular) within the Elohim group. The text supports a divine-council reading equally well; neither is forced.

*Tselem* and *demut* — **image** and **likeness**. The lexical core in Hebrew is **physical** resemblance:

- *Tselem* elsewhere denotes physical statues/representations: Num 33:52 (cast metal images), 1 Sam 6:5 (golden tumours/mice), Ezek 7:20, 16:17 (idol-statues).
- *Demut* elsewhere denotes bodily likeness: Ezek 1:5,10 ("the likeness as the appearance of a man"), 2 Kgs 16:10 (the pattern of an altar), 2 Chron 4:3.

Traditional Jewish and Christian readings spiritualize: humankind bears the Elohim's *moral* or *spiritual* image. The Hebrew lexicon supports physical resemblance **directly**, without interpretive extension. The lens reading is that the lexical core is the load-bearing data; the spiritualizing readings are extensions that may or may not be doing additional work.

paragraphs.text: וַיְבָ֣רֶךְ אֹתָם֮ אֱלֹהִים֒ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר לָהֶ֜ם אֱלֹהִ֗ים פְּר֥וּ וּרְב֛וּ וּמִלְא֥וּ אֶת־הָאָ֖רֶץ וְכִבְשֻׁ֑הָ וּרְד֞וּ בִּדְגַ֤ת הַיָּם֙ וּבְע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וּבְכָל־חַיָּ֖ה הָֽרֹמֶ֥שֶׂת עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim blessed them. And the Elohim said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the land, and subdue it; and rule over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the skies, and over every living thing that moves upon the land."

paragraphs.commentary: *Kivshuha* ("subdue it") and *redu* ("rule") are strong verbs and not softened. *Kavash* in the Qal is forceful — "conquer", "bring under". *Radah* in the Qal denotes dominant rule, occasionally with the spatial sense of treading. Both verbs have been the subject of intense exegetical debate in environmental ethics since Lynn White Jr.'s 1967 thesis ("The Historical Roots of Our Ecologic Crisis"). The WoH translation does not paper over the strength; the interpretive question is a lens question, not a translation one.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֗ים הִנֵּה֩ נָתַ֨תִּי לָכֶ֜ם אֶת־כָּל־עֵ֣שֶׂב ׀ זֹרֵ֣עַ זֶ֗רַע אֲשֶׁר֙ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י כָל־הָאָ֔רֶץ וְאֶת־כָּל־הָעֵ֛ץ אֲשֶׁר־בּ֥וֹ פְרִי־עֵ֖ץ זֹרֵ֣עַ זָ֑רַע לָכֶ֥ם יִֽהְיֶ֖ה לְאָכְלָֽה׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said, "Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant upon the face of all the land, and every tree in which is the fruit of a tree bearing seed; to you it shall be for food.

paragraphs.text: וּֽלְכָל־חַיַּ֣ת הָ֠אָרֶץ וּלְכָל־ע֨וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֜יִם וּלְכֹ֣ל ׀ רוֹמֵ֣שׂ עַל־הָאָ֗רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ֙ נֶ֣פֶשׁ חַיָּ֔ה אֶת־כָּל־יֶ֥רֶק עֵ֖שֶׂב לְאָכְלָ֑ה וַֽיְהִי־כֵֽן׃

i18n.en: And to every living thing of the land, and to every bird of the skies, and to every thing that moves upon the land in which is a living being—every green plant for food." And it was so.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֤רְא אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֔ה וְהִנֵּה־ט֖וֹב מְאֹ֑ד וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם הַשִּׁשִּֽׁי׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And the Elohim saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter closes.** *Yom ha-shishi* — **the sixth day**, with the definite article *ha-*. Days 2–5 lack the article; day 6 has it. The ordinal pattern with definite-article-on-day-6 marks day 6 as the culminating day, parallel to day one being marked by the cardinal *echad*. The numbered-day structure is deliberate and bookended. The closing *tov me'od* ("very good") intensifies the recurring formulaic "good" — six days of *tov*, peaking on day 6 with *tov me'od*.
